claims.claim: Shingles (herpes zoster) is caused by reactivation of varicella-zoster virus, the same virus that causes chickenpox.
After recovery from chickenpox, virus remains inactive in some nerve cells and may reactivate later; why reactivation occurs in some people is not fully understood.
Reactivated virus travels in a specific nerve, commonly producing a band of rash on one side of the trunk; the face can also be affected.
Risk increases with older age and weakened immunity, including certain diseases and immune-suppressing medicines.
Burning or tingling pain, itching or numbness may precede a red rash; fluid-filled blisters then dry and crust, followed by clearing scabs. Timing varies.
Shingles may be painful or itchy; light touch can provoke intense pain in some people.
Postherpetic neuralgia is pain that persists in the affected area after the rash has gone; older people have a greater chance of developing it.
Blisters on the face require prompt medical attention; blisters near or in the eye can cause lasting eye damage and blindness.
If shingles is suspected, contact a clinician as soon as possible. Early antiviral treatment can shorten illness and reduce severity; pain relief may help.
Cool washcloths, loose clothing, keeping the area clean and avoiding scratching can help with comfort and skin care.
A person cannot catch shingles from another person with shingles. VZV can spread from shingles blisters to susceptible people and cause chickenpox.
VZV spread can occur by direct contact with blister fluid or breathing virus particles from blisters. Virus is not spread before blisters appear or after the rash scabs over.

Cover the rash, avoid touching or scratching it, and wash hands. Avoid contact with susceptible pregnant people, premature or low-birth-weight infants and immunocompromised people until the rash scabs over.

CDC recommends two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults age 50 and older and adults age 19 and older with weakened immune systems due to disease or therapy, to prevent shingles and related complications.

claims.claim: The retina is light-sensitive tissue lining the back of the eye; it converts entering light into electrical signals sent to the brain through the optic nerve.
Retinal detachment separates the retina from its normal position at the back wall and underlying blood supply, impairing function and risking permanent vision loss.
In the most common, tear-related (rhegmatogenous) type, fluid passes through a retinal hole or tear and collects beneath the retina, lifting it away.
Aging-related separation of vitreous gel from the retina can cause a retinal tear; thinning peripheral retina and trauma can also lead to tears.
Tractional detachment occurs when scar tissue pulls the retina away; diabetes or other conditions can cause it.
Exudative detachment occurs when leaking vessels allow fluid to accumulate beneath the retina; inflammation or abnormal vessels can be involved.
Warning signs include a sudden increase in floaters, flashes of light, and a dark curtain or shadow in the field of vision; some small detachments cause no symptoms.
Retinal detachment is a medical emergency; symptoms require an eye doctor or emergency room right away, and prompt treatment can help protect vision.
Risk factors include extreme nearsightedness, advancing age, previous eye surgery, serious eye injury, previous detachment, and family history; risk factors do not mean detachment is inevitable.
Diagnosis uses a dilated eye exam to inspect the retina, including its periphery; OCT or ultrasound may help when more information is needed.
Laser or freezing treatment can seal retinal tears; a larger detachment may require surgery to put the retina back into place.
A scleral buckle is a silicone band outside the eye wall that pushes it closer to a retinal tear; freezing treatment seals the tear.
Vitrectomy removes vitreous gel and drains fluid from beneath the retina; laser or freezing seals tears and a gas bubble can hold the retina while it heals.
Pneumatic retinopexy uses a gas bubble and specific head posture to position the bubble over a tear, with laser or freezing to seal it.
A retina specialist selects treatment based on the detachment; more than one procedure may be needed and reattachment does not guarantee complete visual recovery.
The macula is the center of the retina; involvement of this central area affects visual prognosis.
Many aging-related detachments cannot be prevented; protective eyewear during risky activities reduces injury risk and regular dilated eye exams can find small tears or detachments early.

claims.claim: Glaucoma is a group of eye diseases that damage the optic nerve at the back of the eye; lost vision cannot be restored by glaucoma treatment.
The optic nerve contains many nerve fibers; loss of these fibers causes blind spots.
Aqueous fluid in the front of the eye normally leaves through the drainage angle; impaired drainage can increase eye pressure.

In deep ocean water, a tsunami has a long wavelength and often small surface height; it may be barely noticeable.

For a long wave, propagation speed c is approximated by sqrt(g h), where g is gravitational acceleration and h water depth.
As a tsunami enters shallower water, its wavelength decreases.
Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength; slowing propagation does not itself change frequency, so wavelength becomes shorter.
Shoaling is the increase in wave amplitude as a wave moves into shallow water; tsunami waves can grow much taller near the coast.
Currents intensify as tsunamis approach shallow coastal water.
Even after shoaling, tsunami wavelengths remain relatively long; water can continue flowing inland for many minutes.
Run-up refers to the maximum height reached inland above normal sea level, distinct from horizontal inundation extent.

claims.claim: Dental anxiety can occur before a visit; severe persistent dental fear can lead to avoidance. Ordinary nervousness does not itself establish a phobia.
Dental fear can be associated with feared pain, previous difficult experiences, unfamiliar procedures, or a perceived lack of control.
The sights of dental instruments, drilling sounds and vibrations, clinical smells, and the reclined dental-chair position can trigger anxiety for some people.
Uncertainty about what will happen can contribute to anxiety; asking questions about the procedure can help reduce fear of the unknown.
Possible anxiety responses include a noticeable heartbeat, trembling, dizziness, chest tightness, feeling sick, muscle tension and sweaty palms; symptoms vary.
Avoiding dental care can increase the risk of dental problems and make later visits more difficult, reinforcing fear; this is a possible cycle, not an inevitable outcome.
Fear can concern perceived danger; pain concerns should not be dismissed. Patients should discuss pain management and tell the dentist if pain occurs even with local anesthetic.
Tell the dental team about anxiety and previous experiences; ask what will happen and agree on a raised-hand signal to pause.
Headphones for bothersome drilling sounds, a handheld stress ball, slow breathing and relaxing tense muscles can help manage dental anxiety.
CBT and professionally guided exposure-based approaches can help with dental phobia; management should be tailored to the person and clinical situation.
Seek professional help when phobia symptoms affect life; a dentist and mental-health professional may work together on care.

claims.claim: Arachnophobia is fear of spiders, a type of specific phobia.
Phobic fear can be intense and out of proportion to actual danger.
Seeing the feared object can cause immediate anxiety; anticipation and even thinking about it can also cause anxiety.
Some people with arachnophobia avoid touching a spider; some cannot look at a spider picture.
Physical symptoms can include palpitations, chest tightness, trembling, dizziness and nausea; experiences vary.
People may actively avoid feared objects and organise life around avoidance, limiting daily activities.
A repeated encounter can provoke anxiety again; avoidance and intense anxiety are common features, not proof of actual danger.
It is not always clear why a phobia develops; frightening experiences and learned fear can be involved.
CBT is an effective treatment; exposure therapy is a CBT method particularly effective for phobias.
Exposure treatment can involve gradually becoming exposed to the feared object; plans differ and a specialist can help.
Breathing exercises and talking to a trusted person may help manage symptoms, and triggering images may be distressing.
Seek a primary care or qualified mental health professional when symptoms interfere with life.

Gallstones are hard pebble-like material formed in the gallbladder; cholesterol stones are typically yellow-green and pigment stones are dark and made of bilirubin.

Most gallstones are silent and do not cause symptoms; asymptomatic gallbladder stones usually need no treatment.
A stone obstructing a bile duct can cause bile buildup and biliary colic; attacks often stop when the stone moves and the blockage ends.

Persistent blockage can lead to gallbladder inflammation, bile-duct infection, or gallstone pancreatitis; these are possible complications, not inevitable outcomes.
Risk is higher with older age, family history, obesity, rapid weight loss, and in women; risk factors do not establish an individual diagnosis.
Evaluation of suspected gallstones can include ultrasound and blood tests; similar symptoms may have other causes requiring clinical assessment.
The main treatment for symptomatic gallstones is gallbladder removal, often laparoscopic; ERCP may clear a stone in the common bile duct. Treatment depends on clinical circumstances.
After gallbladder removal, bile flows from the liver through the ducts directly into the duodenum rather than being stored in a gallbladder.

Healthy eating with fiber, regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight and avoiding rapid weight loss can help reduce gallstone risk; they do not guarantee prevention or dissolve existing stones.

Use a magnifier linking the elbow outline to the cross-section, fine layer outlines, and a clear arrow legend. The diagram must not imply an opening through the whole skin or a single universal genetic cause.

Arrange EIGHT numbered supporting panels in a well-spaced, two-column grid around and below the hero. Each explains something distinct. Include at least four explanatory diagrams or close-ups overall.

1. "BARRIER & ITCH". A close-up of the orderly versus less orderly outer-layer cells, beside a four-step circular arrow diagram: "Inflammation → itch → scratching → further irritation". Show abstract symbols only, not a hand scratching skin. Small text "Scratching can increase infection risk". Do not imply every itchy patch is infected.

2. "HOW SYMPTOMS VARY". Three softly shaded, abstract skin-tone swatches, light, medium and dark, with restrained symbolic color patches rather than realistic symptom textures. Labels "Itchy", "Dry or cracked", "Scaly or thickened". Explain "Color varies with skin tone" and "May look red, purple, grey, lighter or darker". Do not imply each skin tone has one fixed symptom color. Keep comparison windows equal in size and visual importance.

3. "WHERE & WHEN". Small neutral human-outline diagrams with clean location markers and no bodily detail. Text "Babies: often face", "Children/adults: often folds and hands", "Can occur elsewhere". Use a simple head outline for facial location and separate elbow, knee and hand outlines for the other markers, not portraits of affected patients. An undulating schematic timeline reads "Flares ↔ improvement"; a moon-and-pillow icon reads "Itch may disrupt sleep". No numerical axis.

4. "WHY FLARES VARY". Detailed everyday object icons: unscented-care versus fragrance symbol, detergent bottle, wool-fabric weave, warm-air lines, and a stress-cloud symbol. Caption "Personal triggers differ". A three-part diagram reads "Genes + immune system + environment". A small family-tree icon reads "Family history raises likelihood" with "eczema, asthma or hay fever" beneath. Show association, not a claim that allergies alone cause eczema.

5. "HOW IT IS ASSESSED". A stylized clinician and a fully clothed adult consulting at a small abstract desk; beside them, a magnifying-glass icon over an undamaged elbow outline and a history-card diagram. Labels "Skin examination", "Symptoms & sleep", "Family and trigger history". Note "Tests may help rule out other causes". No self-diagnosis scoring or promise of one definitive test.

6. "EVERYDAY BARRIER CARE". Three-step illustrated sequence using a basin, folded towel and neutral pump bottle: "Lukewarm water + gentle cleanser" → "Pat gently" → "Moisturize damp skin". An explanatory micro-diagram shows a smooth moisturizer layer above the same geometric skin model and fewer upward water arrows; label "Moisturizers help retain water". Add "Avoid personal irritants • Keep cool • Short nails" and "Do not change diet without clinical advice". No brands or home-treatment recipes.

7. "TREAT THE INFLAMMATION". A clinician-guided options diagram with a plain cream tube and light-therapy equipment symbol, without depicting treatment on a person. Main labels "Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation", "Other clinician-selected options", "Choice depends on age, severity and response", "Control symptoms; no current cure". These are educational options, not directions to start treatment. A fabric-and-fire-safety symbol accompanies "Emollient residue on fabrics: keep away from flames". No doses or blanket treatment advice.

8. "WHEN TO GET HELP". Calm amber information panel using a phone, medical cross and thermometer icons. Warning signs are TEXT ONLY; do not illustrate symptoms here. Readable lines "Urgent medical advice: painful warm swelling, pus, sudden worsening, new blisters, fever or feeling unwell" and "May signal infection, including eczema herpeticum". Separate routine-care line "Seek care if symptoms persist or treatment is not helping". Ordinary dry skin alone is not presented as an emergency. No antibiotic instructions.

Readable footer: "General education • Individual care needs clinical assessment". Produce a sophisticated and richly illustrated science-museum educational plate with crisp typography, clean diagrammatic anatomy, clear causal arrows and substantive content. Preserve every numbered panel and its distinct purpose; favor legibility and medical accuracy over decorative density. No unsupported claims.

claims.claim: Atopic dermatitis is a chronic inflammatory skin disease, often starting in childhood but possible at any age; it is not contagious.
Barrier changes allow moisture to escape and expose the skin immune system to the environment; genes, immune activity and environmental factors contribute, and there is no single known cause.
Skin has a protective outer layer; a schematic intact-versus-disrupted surface comparison illustrates moisture retention versus increased water loss, not a literal hole through the whole skin.
Inflammation can trigger itch; scratching causes further skin damage and inflammation and increases bacterial infection risk.
Symptoms include intense itching, dryness, cracking, scaling and thickened skin; scratches may bleed or weep clear fluid.
Eczema appearance varies with skin tone: it can appear red, purple, grey or lighter or darker than surrounding skin; inflammation may leave color changes.
Common sites include elbow and knee bends and hands; babies often have facial eczema. Distribution varies by age and can occur elsewhere.
Symptoms fluctuate between flares and improvement; itch can disturb sleep.
Family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever is associated with increased likelihood, not proof of one cause.
Soap, detergents, fragrances, rough fabrics, heat and stress may worsen symptoms; triggers vary by person.
Diagnosis involves clinical skin examination and medical, family and trigger history; clinicians may use tests to rule out other causes.
Regular moisturizing, including immediately after bathing, helps retain water and supports the skin barrier; gentle unscented or non-soap cleansing and lukewarm water can help.
Avoid personal irritants, keep cool and keep nails short to reduce scratching damage; do not change diet unless advised by a clinician.

Topical corticosteroids reduce inflammation; other topical treatments, phototherapy or systemic medicines may be considered by clinicians depending on severity, age and response, not as universal treatments.
Treatment can control symptoms but there is currently no cure; seek care for symptoms or treatments that are not helping.

Painful warm swollen skin, pus, sudden worsening or spreading, fever or feeling unwell, and new blisters or leaking/crusting can signal infection or eczema herpeticum and warrant urgent medical advice.
Emollients transferred onto clothing, bedding or dressings can make fabrics catch fire more easily; avoid smoking and naked flames.
